clue.text: Madeleine reminded him

parts.note: a madeleine cake dipped in tea famously brought back childhood memories to the French author of In Search of Lost Time

explanation.surface: Someone called Madeleine jogs a man's memory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madeleine' reads as a woman's name, but it is the small shell-shaped cake whose taste opens the great French memory novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist built his whole book on the involuntary memory a small cake dipped in tea set off.

clue.text: English recorder of French lives with German car

parts.note: mit is the German word for with
a Ford is a make of car

explanation.surface: An English biographer of French figures travels in a German car.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy Mitford, English writer, wrote lives of Madame de Pompadour, Voltaire and Louis XIV.
explanation.definitionFit: Nancy Mitford wrote biographies of Pompadour, Voltaire and the Sun King, all French subjects.

clue.text: Chaucerian tale-teller as gothic novelist

definitions.meaning: one of the Canterbury pilgrims, a manor steward, tells his own story
Clara ... wrote The Old English Baron, an early gothic romance

explanation.surface: A Canterbury pilgrim moonlights as a writer of gothic novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's steward pilgrim tells a tale, and Clara of that surname wrote gothic fiction.

clue.text: Upwards with tall poet?

definitions.meaning: the Latin motto means ever higher
a tall poet is a Long fellow, so this points to the famous Longfellow poem of that title

explanation.surface: Climbing in the company of a lanky versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: A tall poet is a 'long fellow': Longfellow, whose poem has a youth carrying a banner marked with this Latin word up a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word means higher, ever upward, and is also the title of a Longfellow poem.

clue.text: Little sparrow with no regrets

parts.note: the French singer was nicknamed the little sparrow and sang Non, je ne regrette rien

explanation.surface: A small bird that feels no remorse.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'little sparrow' is the French singer's nickname, from Parisian slang for a sparrow; 'with no regrets' recalls her song Non, je ne regrette rien.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith, the French chanteuse, bore the slang name for sparrow and sang that she regretted nothing.

clue.text: London venue's exhibition of Macedonian queen

definitions.meaning: Olympia is an exhibition hall in west London, here in the possessive
the wife of Philip II and mother of Alexander the Great

explanation.surface: A London exhibition hall puts on a show about an ancient queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Olympia is a large exhibition centre in west London; 'exhibition of' joins its possessive to the queen, mother of Alexander the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: The Macedonian consort of Philip II shares her name with a London exhibition hall plus possessive S.

clue.text: French novelist of The Cobra's Return?

indicators.note: Return as a title word here means the cobra's name is read backwards

parts.note: a naga is a cobra in Indian myth, so the cobra's gives naga's

explanation.surface: A French writer seems to have penned a snake thriller sequel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' tells you to read NAGAS (naga's, the cobra's) backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Francoise Sagan was the French author of Bonjour Tristesse.

clue.text: When I want to read a novel, I write one " he said

definitions.text: When I want to read a novel, I write one " he said

parts.words: When I want to read a novel, I write one " he said
parts.note: a famous remark attributed to the Victorian prime minister who also wrote novels such as Sybil

explanation.surface: A writer explains how he gets his reading matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The quip is attributed to Benjamin Disraeli, British prime minister and author of novels including Coningsby and Sybil.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian statesman-novelist is credited with this line about writing a novel to read one.

clue.text: Mark's wife not so young, we're told

indicators.note: we're told signals that the words are heard spoken rather than spelt out

parts.note: someone not so young ..., so the phrase reads as ...

explanation.surface: Someone's wife is reported to be past her youth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is older', said without the final R as in British speech, sounds like the name; King Mark of Cornwall married Isolde.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Tristan legend the Irish princess marries King Mark of Cornwall.

clue.text: New Troy cache reveals government like that of the Incas

definitions.text: government like that of the Incas

indicators.note: something new is remade, so the letters of these words are formed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A hoard found at Troy sheds light on how the Incas were ruled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges TROY CACHE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca emperor was held divine, so the state was ruled by a god-king: rule by religion.

clue.text: Roman jurist happy in Paris and America

parts.note: gai is the French for happy or cheerful
US is the abbreviation for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A Roman lawyer is content both in France and the States.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius wrote the Institutes, a classic textbook of Roman law in the second century.

clue.text: A single sick playwright

parts.note: a single thing is one
sick means ill

explanation.surface: A lone dramatist is unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill was the American dramatist of Long Day's Journey into Night.

clue.text: Reds plan unusual architectural feature

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of the words before it appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Communists draw up an odd building design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges REDS PLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The curved triangular space between an arch and its frame is this feature of buildings.

clue.text: Make sudden move, that is like Galsworthian rogue

parts.note: to dart is to make a sudden move
i.e., from Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A Galsworthy villain leaps forward suddenly.
explanation.walkthrough: Montague Dartie is the dissolute husband of Winifred in Galsworthy's The Forsyte Saga.
explanation.definitionFit: Montague of that surname is the gambling, philandering scoundrel in The Forsyte Saga.

clue.text: Aristotelian theme might be bombast

definitions.meaning: Aristotle wrote a treatise on the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: A subject Aristotle treated might turn out to be hot air.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle's treatise on persuasive speaking bears this name, which also means empty grandiloquence.

clue.text: Dancing girl in ballet

definitions.meaning: A ballet by Minkus and Petipa

explanation.surface: A girl dances in a ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: The French term for an Indian temple dancer is also the title of Petipa's ballet.

clue.text: Reconciliation in one day by Al Alvarez

definitions.meaning: Al Alvarez wrote a novel called Day of ...

explanation.surface: Making peace in a single day, as written by Al Alvarez.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Alvarez, British poet and critic, published the novel Day of Atonement (1991); 'one day by' points to that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Reconciliation and making amends are the sense of the word in Al Alvarez's novel title Day of ....

clue.text: He said that he wrote with Aunt Edna in mind

definitions.text: He said that he wrote with Aunt Edna in mind

parts.words: He said that he wrote with Aunt Edna in mind
parts.note: a twentieth-century English playwright invented Aunt Edna as his typical conventional theatregoer

explanation.surface: A writer keeps his elderly aunt in mind as he works.
explanation.walkthrough: Terence Rattigan, English playwright of The Winslow Boy, said he wrote for 'Aunt Edna', an imagined respectable middle-class playgoer.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright of The Browning Version coined Aunt Edna as his imagined audience member.

clue.text: Kafkaesque work of Yonge?

definitions.meaning: Kafka's novel about Josef K's prosecution
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote a novel with the same title

explanation.surface: A nightmarish book perhaps by a Victorian lady novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte Yonge, Victorian novelist, wrote The Trial (1864), a sequel to The Daisy Chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Kafka's Der Process is known in English by this title, also used by Charlotte Yonge for a novel.

clue.text: Burned (while topless), Marlowe reports

parts.note: Marlowe's Faustus speaks of the face that burnt the topless structures of Ilium

explanation.surface: A Marlowe news item about something burning while unclothed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests nudity, but in Doctor Faustus it means too high to see the top: Helen's face 'burnt the topless towers of Ilium'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlowe's line describes Troy's tall buildings, so high their tops were out of sight, set on fire.

clue.text: Wilde lord found by the sea in Sussex

definitions.meaning: Lord ... is the dandy in An Ideal Husband
...-by-Sea is a place on the Sussex coast

explanation.surface: A Wilde nobleman turns up at the seaside in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Goring-by-Sea is a resort near Worthing on the Sussex coast in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's dandy Lord in An Ideal Husband shares his name with a Sussex seaside village.

clue.text: Example coming up about demand to students from novelist

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes around the next
in a down clue coming up means read from bottom to top, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: e.g. is short for for example
to demand is to ask
L is a learner, so two students give two Ls

explanation.surface: An instance arises of a novelist making demands on pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'coming up' reads the example abbreviation upwards, and 'about' wraps it round the demand; the two learner plates follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Gaskell was the Victorian author of Cranford and North and South.

clue.text: "… Fancy's child, / Warble his natives — - — wild" (Milton)

definitions.text: "… Fancy's child, / Warble his natives — - — wild" (Milton)

parts.words: "… Fancy's child, / Warble his natives — - — wild" (Milton)
parts.note: the gap is filled from Milton's L'Allegro, where Shakespeare, Fancy's child, warbles native woodland songs

explanation.surface: A gap-fill quotation from Milton's L'Allegro about Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: In L'Allegro, Milton calls Shakespeare 'Fancy's child' who warbles 'his native wood-notes wild'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's phrase for Shakespeare's untaught poetry compares it to birdsong in the forest.

clue.text: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring

definitions.text: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring

parts.words: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring
parts.note: the Elizabethan pamphleteer wrote Lenten Stuffe in praise of the red herring of Yarmouth

explanation.surface: A writer's Lent fare was a misleading clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red herring' suggests a false trail, but Thomas Nashe's Lenten Stuffe (1599) is a mock praise of the smoked herring of Great Yarmouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan satirist Thomas wrote Lenten Stuffe extolling Yarmouth's cured fish.

clue.text: He was seen as inimitable, yet in the offing

definitions.meaning: Wodehouse's book The Inimitable ... features the valet
Wodehouse also wrote ... in the Offing

explanation.surface: Someone unique is still on the horizon.
explanation.walkthrough: Both phrases are Wodehouse titles, The Inimitable Jeeves and Jeeves in the Offing, about Bertie Wooster's valet.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie Wooster's resourceful valet appears in Wodehouse titles calling him inimitable and in the offing.

clue.text: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop

definitions.text: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop

parts.words: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop
parts.note: a curiosity shop holds curios and objets d'art, collectively a taste for fine antiques

explanation.surface: What fills Dickens's novel set in an antiques shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contents' looks like the chapters of Dickens's novel, but means the stock of such a shop: curios and objects of art.
explanation.definitionFit: The word denotes curios and antique art objects collectively, the stock of a curiosity dealer.

clue.text: Heroic narrative, mostly from 6

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word is kept, so its final letter is lost

parts.note: the answer to 6 down is the French novelist's surname

explanation.surface: A heroic tale largely taken from another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of SAGAN, the answer to 6 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse and Icelandic prose stories of heroes and families are called by this name.

clue.text: Macaulay derived pleasure from them

parts.note: Rose Macaulay wrote the book Pleasure of ..., about crumbling ancient sites

explanation.surface: A historian enjoyed something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Macaulay' suggests the historian Lord Macaulay, but it is Rose Macaulay, whose 1953 book is Pleasure of Ruins.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Macaulay's book celebrates the pleasure of decayed ancient buildings.

clue.text: Rosamond Lehmann's fruit-bearer from The Sea

definitions.text: Rosamond Lehmann's fruit-bearer from The Sea

parts.words: Rosamond Lehmann's fruit-bearer from The Sea
parts.note: Lehmann's novel The Sea-... Tree names a coastal plant that bears clusters of fruit

explanation.surface: A novelist's fruit-bearing plant comes from the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosamond Lehmann's 1976 novel is The Sea-Grape Tree; take away 'The Sea' to leave the fruit-bearer.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea grape is a coastal tree bearing grape-like clusters, the title of Lehmann's novel.

clue.text: 1ac personage, sort of a lean Justine

indicators.note: sort of here means a sorting of the letters, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Proust character is a kind of slimmer Justine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges A LEAN JUSTINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Santeuil is the hero of Proust's early unfinished novel, named after him.
